text: A police‑officer may arrest a person without a warrant when the person is suspected of a cognizable offence and the arrest is necessary for specified reasons. Specifically, the officer may arrest (i) anyone who commits a cognizable offence in the officer’s presence, or (ii) anyone against whom a reasonable complaint, credible information or reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years, provided the officer believes the person committed the offence and the arrest is needed to prevent further offence, to investigate properly, to preserve evidence or to stop intimidation of witnesses. The officer may also arrest without warrant in other situations listed in the statute, such as a person against whom credible information shows a cognizable offence punishable by more than seven years or death, a person possessing an implement of house‑breaking without lawful excuse, a proclaimed offender, a person found with suspected stolen property, anyone obstructing a police‑officer, a suspected deserter, a person involved in an act committed abroad that would be an offence in Bangladesh, a released convict breaching certain rules, or when a requisition for arrest has been received from another police‑officer. However, the officer may not arrest for the purpose of preventive detention.

citations.quote: Any police-officer may, without an order from a Magistrate and without warrant, arrest- firstly, any person who commits, in the presence of a police-officer, a cognizable offence; secondly, any person against whom a reasonable complaint has been made, or credible information has been received, or a reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence ... if the following conditions are satisfied, namely:- (i) the police-officer has reason to believe ... and (ii) the police-officer is satisfied that such arrest is necessary- (a) to prevent such person from committing any further offence; or (b) for proper investigation of the offence; or (c) to prevent such person from causing the evidence of the offence to disappear ...

thirdly, any person against whom credible information has been received that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to more than seven years whether with or without fine, or with death sentence ... fourthly, any person having in his possession without lawful excuse ... implement of house breaking; fifthly, any person who has been proclaimed as an offender ... sixthly, any person in whose possession anything is found which may reasonably be suspected to be stolen property ... seventhly, any person who obstructs a police-officer while in the execution of his duty ... eighthly, any person who is reasonably suspected of being a deserter ... ninthly, any person who has been concerned in ... act committed at any place out of Bangladesh ... tenthly, any released convict ... eleventhly, any person for whose arrest a requisition, has been received from another police-officer
No police-officer shall arrest a person under this section for the purpose of detaining him under any law providing for preventive detention.

text: Police may detain a person arrested without a warrant for up to twenty‑four hours (excluding travel time to the Magistrate’s Court) unless a special order is obtained under section 167. They must otherwise bring the arrested person before a Magistrate without unnecessary delay.

citations.quote: shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 167, exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court.

shall, without unnecessary delay and subject to the provisions herein contained as to bail, take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police-station.

text: The search of a woman must be carried out by another woman, as required by the Code of Criminal Procedure.

citations.quote: Whenever it is necessary to cause a woman to be searched, the search shall be made by another woman, with strict regard to decency.
If such person is a woman, the directions of section 52 shall be observed.

text: A person who has been arrested may be restrained only to the extent necessary to prevent his escape; no greater restraint is permitted.

citations.quote: The person arrested shall not be subjected to more restraint than is necessary to prevent his escape.

text: When making an arrest a police officer must: bear an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name; disclose his identity and, if asked, show his identity card to the arrested person and any others present; prepare a memorandum of arrest that is attested by a suitable witness and countersigned or thumb‑impressed by the arrested person; inform a family member, relative or nominated friend of the arrest within 24 hours, giving details of time, place and custody; if the arrested person has any injury, ensure medical examination and first‑aid treatment, obtain a medical certificate and record the reasons for the injury; and allow the arrested person, if desired, to consult a lawyer of his choice or meet a close relation, preferably within twelve hours.

citations.quote: (a) bear an accurate, visible and clear identification of his name which will facilitate easy identification;
(b) disclose his identity and if demanded, shall show his identity card to the person arrested and to the persons present at the time of arrest;

(c) prepare a memorandum of arrest which shall be- (i)attested by at least one witness, who is a member of the family of the person arrested or a respectable inhabitant of the locality where the arrest is made and where no such witness is available, the reasons thereof be recorded in the memorandum; (ii) countersigned or thumb-impressed by the person arrested if not refused by him;

(d) intimate, where the accused is arrested from a place other than his residence, to a family member, relative, or a friend nominated by the person arrested, as soon as practicable but not later than twenty four hours from the time of such arrest, notifying the time and place of arrest and the place of custody;

(e) ensure, if any mark of injury is found on the body of the person arrested, the examination and first aid treatment of the person by a medical officer or a registered medical practitioner, as the case may be, in accordance with section 46E; obtain a certificate from the attending medical officer or practitioner; and record the reasons for such injury;
(f) allow the person arrested, if he so desires, to consult a lawyer of his choice or to meet any of his nearest relation, preferably within twelve hours of such arrest.

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, a police officer who arrests a person without a warrant must, at the time of the arrest, tell the person the reasons for which he is being arrested.

citations.quote: Every police-officer arresting any person without warrant shall, at the time of making arrest, communicate to him the reasons for which he is arrested.

text: When information about a cognizable offence is given to the officer in charge of a police‑station, the officer must put the oral information in writing (or have it written under his direction), read it back to the informant, have the informant sign it, and then enter the substance of the information in a book kept by the officer in the form prescribed by the Government.

citations.quote: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence if given orally to an officer in charge of a police‑station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the Government may prescribe in this behalf.

text: No. Under section 155(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a police officer may not investigate a non‑cognizable case unless he has an order from a Magistrate of the first or second class having power to try the case.

citations.quote: No police-officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate of the first or second class having power to try such case

text: Yes. An officer in charge of a police‑station can investigate a cognizable case without a Magistrate’s order.

citations.quote: Any officer in charge of a police-station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case

text: Yes. Section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure allows a police officer conducting an investigation to issue a written order requiring any person who appears to be acquainted with the case to attend before him.

citations.quote: Any police-officer making an investigation under this Chapter may, by order in writing, require the attendance before himself of any person ... who, from the information given or otherwise, appears to be acquainted with the circumstances of the case; and such person shall attend as so required.

text: No. A person examined by a police officer is bound to answer all questions except those whose answers would tend to expose him to a criminal charge, penalty, or forfeiture.

citations.quote: Such person shall be bound to answer all questions relating to such case put to him by such officer, other than questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture.

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, a statement made to a police officer during an investigation must not be signed by the person making it.

citations.quote: No statement made by any person to a police-officer in the course of an investigation under this Chapter shall, if reduced into writing, be signed by the person making it;

text: No. A police officer is prohibited from offering any inducement, threat or promise to obtain a statement.

citations.quote: No police-officer or other person in authority shall offer or make, or cause to be offered or made, any such inducement, threat or promise as is mentioned in the Evidence Act, 1872, section 24.

text: A confession may be recorded by any Metropolitan Magistrate, any Magistrate of the first class, or any Magistrate of the second class who has been specially empowered by the Government, provided the magistrate is not a police‑officer. Before recording the confession, the magistrate must explain to the person that he is not bound to make a confession and that, if he does, the confession may be used as evidence against him.

citations.quote: Any Metropolitan Magistrate, any Magistrate of the first class and any Magistrate of the second class specially empowered in this behalf by the Government may, if he is not a police-officer record any statement or confession
A Magistrate shall, before recording any such confession, explain to the person making it that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he does so it may be used as evidence against him

text: If, after a person is arrested, the police determine that the investigation cannot be finished within the 24‑hour period prescribed by section 61, the officer in charge must immediately send a copy of the diary entries to the nearest Judicial Magistrate and forward the accused to that magistrate. The magistrate may then order a medical examination of the accused, produce the accused before the magistrate without delay, and, if injury or alleged torture is shown, direct another medical examination. The magistrate can also authorize detention of the accused in police custody for up to fifteen days (or forward the accused to a magistrate with jurisdiction), but lower‑class magistrates cannot authorize such detention. For offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or more than ten years, the Court of Session may release the accused on bail.

citations.quote: Whenever any person is arrested and detained in custody, and it appears that the investigation cannot be completed within the period of twenty-four hours fixed by section 61, ... the officer ... shall forthwith transmit ... a copy of the entries in the diary ... and shall at the same time forward the accused to such Magistrate.

may order that the accused be examined by a medical officer of nearest government hospital before he is handed over to such custody; and upon expiry of the period of police custody, the accused shall be produced before the Magistrate without unnecessary delay; and if, upon such production, there appears to be any mark of injury ... the Magistrate shall direct that the accused be examined by a medical officer ...

The Magistrate ... may ... authorize the detention of the accused in such custody ... for a term not exceeding fifteen days in the whole; and if he has not jurisdiction to try the case ... he may order the accused to be forwarded to a Magistrate having such jurisdiction.

(b) the Court of Session may, if the offence to which the investigation relates is punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment exceeding ten years, release the accused on bail to the satisfaction of such Court

text: A Magistrate may take cognizance of an offence (a) upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute the offence; (b) upon a written report of such facts made by a police‑officer; or (c) upon information from any person other than a police‑officer, or on his own knowledge or suspicion that the offence has been committed.

citations.quote: may take cognizance of any offence- (a) upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute such offence; (b) upon a report in writing of such facts made by any police-officer; (c) upon information received from any person other than a police-officer, or upon his own knowledge or suspicion, that such offence has been committed.

text: When a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence on a complaint, he must immediately examine the complainant (and any witnesses present) on oath, reduce the substance of that examination to writing and have it signed by the complainant or witness and by the Magistrate. However, if the complaint is made in writing, the statute does not require such an examination.

citations.quote: A Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence on complaint shall at once examine ... and the substance of the examination shall be reduced to writing and shall be signed ...
when the complaint is made in writing, nothing herein contained shall be deemed to require [such examination]

text: A Magistrate may postpone issuing process against the person complained about when, on receiving a complaint of an offence he is authorised to take cognizance of (or one transferred to him), he thinks it appropriate and records the reasons in writing. This postponement is allowed provided that, unless the complaint was made by a Court, the requirements of section 200 have been complied with, and it may also be done when the offence is triable exclusively by a Court of Session.

citations.quote: may, if he thinks fit, for reasons to be recorded in writing, postpone the issue of process for compelling the attendance of the person complained against
Provided further that where it appears to the Magistrate that the offence complained of is triable exclusively by a Court of Session, the Magistrate may postpone the issue of process

text: A Magistrate may dismiss a complaint when, after considering the complainant’s statement on oath (if any) and the result of any investigation or inquiry, he judges that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding.

citations.quote: may dismiss the complaint, if after considering the statement on oath (if any) of the complainant and the result of the investigation or inquiry (if any) there is in his judgment no sufficient ground for proceeding.

text: An accused must be discharged before a charge is framed when the magistrate finds the charge to be groundless, or when the public prosecutor withdraws the prosecution before a charge is framed. In the first case the magistrate, after considering the record and hearing both sides, may discharge the accused if he considers the charge groundless. In the second case, if the prosecutor withdraws the case before a charge is framed, the accused is to be discharged.

citations.quote: considers the charge to be groundless, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing.
if it is made before a charge has been framed, the accused shall be discharged in respect of such offence or offences

text: If the complainant does not appear on the day set for the accused’s appearance (or any adjourned day), the magistrate must acquit the accused, unless the magistrate decides to adjourn the hearing to another day. An exception is made when the complainant is a public servant whose personal attendance is not required; in that case the magistrate may dispense with his attendance and continue with the case.

citations.quote: the complainant does not appear, the Magistrate shall, notwithstanding anything herein before contained, acquit the accused, unless for some reason he thinks proper to adjoin the hearing of the case to some other day
where the complainant is a public servant and his personal attendance is not required, the Magistrate may dispense with his attendance, and proceed with the case

text: When a Magistrate is satisfied that an accusation was false and either frivolous or vexatious, he may order the complainant or informant to pay compensation to the accused, may summon the complainant to show cause why he should not pay, and may impose further penalties such as imprisonment for default of payment, additional imprisonment or a fine. Specifically, the Magistrate can direct compensation to be paid (section 250), call upon the complainant to show cause or issue a summons (section 250 (1)), order simple imprisonment for up to thirty days for non‑payment (section 250 (2A)), and may also order imprisonment for up to six months or a fine of up to one lac taka in addition to the compensation order (section 250 (5)).

citations.quote: if he is satisfied that the accusation was false and either frivolous or vexatious ... direct that compensation ... be paid by such complainant or informant to the accused
call upon him forthwith to show cause why he should not pay compensation to such accused ... or ... direct the issue of a summons to him to appear and show cause as aforesaid

The Magistrate may, by the order directing payment of the compensation under sub-section (2), further order that, in default of payment, the person ordered to pay such compensation shall suffer simple imprisonment for a period not exceeding thirty days

the Magistrate may, in addition to the order directing payment of the compensation under sub-section (2), further order that the person ordered to pay such compensation shall also suffer imprisonment for a period not exceeding six months or pay a fine not exceeding one lac taka

text: A Metropolitan Magistrate or any Magistrate of the first class may tender a pardon to an accomplice, but only in certain offences: those triable exclusively by the Court of Session; offences punishable with imprisonment up to ten years; offences punishable under section 211 of the Penal Code (up to seven years); and offences under sections 216A, 369, 401, 435 and 477A of the Penal Code. The power is limited by the following conditions: if the offence is under inquiry or trial, only the Chief Judicial Magistrate may use the power unless the magistrate is the one conducting the inquiry or trial; if the offence is under investigation, the magistrate must have jurisdiction where the offence could be inquired into or tried and must obtain the sanction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

citations.quote: any Magistrate of the first class may, at any state of the investigation or inquiry into, or the trial of the offence ... tender a pardon to such person

In the case of any offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session, or any offence punishable with imprisonment which may extend to ten years, or any offence punishable under section 211 of the Penal Code, with imprisonment which may extend to seven years, or any offence under any of the following sections of the Penal Code, namely, sections 216A, 369, 401, 435 and 477A, [a Metropolitan Magistrate] or any Magistrate of the first class may ...

Provided that, where the offence is under inquiry or trial, no Magistrate of the first class other than the Chief Judicial Magistrate shall exercise the power ... unless he is the Magistrate making the inquiry or holding the trial, and, where the offence is under investigation, no such Magistrate shall exercise the said power unless ... the sanction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate has been obtained

text: An accused may be tried in his absence when the court has reason to believe he has absconded or is hiding so that he cannot be arrested and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, and after a published direction to appear he fails to comply; also when, after having appeared or been released on bail, the accused later absconds or fails to appear, the court may record its decision and try him in his absence; and when the judge or magistrate is satisfied, for recorded reasons, that the accused is incapable of remaining before the court and the accused is represented by an advocate, the court may dispense with his attendance and proceed with the trial in his absence. In such cases the court may also examine witnesses and record their depositions in the accused’s absence.

citations.quote: where the Court has reason to believe that an accused person has absconded ... and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him ... if such person fails to comply with such direction, he shall be tried in his absence

Where in a case after the production or appearance of an accused before the Court or his release on bail, the accused person absconds or fails to appear ... the Court ... shall, recording its decision so to do, try such person in his absence.

if the Judge or Magistrate is satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, that any one or more of ... accused is ... incapable of remaining before the Court, he may, if such accused is represented by an advocate, dispense with his attendance and proceed ... in his absence
If it is proved that an accused person has absconded, and that there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, the Court ... may, in his absence, examine the witnesses

text: Yes. Under section 485 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a court may imprison or commit a person who refuses to answer questions or produce documents when ordered, for up to seven days.

citations.quote: If any witness or person called to produce a document or thing before a Criminal Court refuses to answer such questions ... such Court may ... sentence him to simple imprisonment, or ... commit him ... for any term not exceeding seven days

text: Yes. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure a criminal court is deemed an open Court and the public generally may have access, although the presiding Judge or Magistrate can, if he thinks fit, order that the public or any particular person be excluded.

citations.quote: The place in which any Criminal Court is held ... shall be deemed an open Court, to which the public generally may have access, ... Provided that the presiding Judge or Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, order ... that the public generally, or any particular person, shall not have access ...

text: No. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure a person who has been acquitted (or convicted) of an offence cannot be tried again for the same offence while that acquittal remains in force.

citations.quote: A person who has once been tried by a Court of competent jurisdiction for an offence and convicted or acquitted of such offence shall, while such conviction or acquittal remains in force, not be liable to be tried again for the same offence

text: An appeal against an order of acquittal may be presented either by the Government, which can direct the Public Prosecutor to file the appeal, or, where the acquittal arises from a case instituted on a complaint and involves an error of law, the complainant himself may present the appeal.

citations.quote: the Government may, in any case, direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal
the complainant may present an appeal

text: The High Court Division may, whenever it thinks fit, issue directions to: (a) bring a person within the limits of its appellate criminal jurisdiction before the Court to be dealt with according to law; (b) set at liberty a person who is illegally or improperly detained in public or private custody; (c) bring a prisoner detained in any jail within those limits before the Court to be examined as a witness in any matter pending or to be inquired into; (d) bring a prisoner detained as aforesaid before a Court‑martial or any Commissioners for trial or to be examined touching any matter pending before such Court‑martial or Commissioners; (e) remove a prisoner within such limits from one custody to another for the purpose of trial.

citations.quote: (a) that a person within the limits of its appellate criminal jurisdiction be brought up before the Court to be dealt with according to law
(b) that a person illegally or improperly detained in public or private custody with such limits be set at liberty
(c) that a prisoner detained in any jail situate within such limits be brought before the Court to be there examined as a witness in any matter pending or to be inquired into in such Court

(d) that a prisoner detained as aforesaid be brought before a Court-martial or any Commissioners for trial or to be examined touching any matter pending before such Court-martial or Commissioners respectively
(e) that a prisoner within such limits be removed from one custody to another for the purpose of trial

text: Yes. Under section 496 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a person who is not accused of a non‑bailable offence (i.e., accused of a bailable offence) and who is prepared to give bail must be released on bail, although the officer or Court may instead accept a bond without sureties.

citations.quote: such person shall be released on bail: Provided that such officer or Court, if he or it thinks fit, may, instead of taking bail from such person, discharge him on his executing a bond without sureties

text: Bail may be granted to a person accused of a non‑bailable offence when the person is arrested or detained without warrant, or appears before a court, provided there are no reasonable grounds for believing he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life. The court may still grant bail to a person under sixteen years of age, a woman, or a sick or infirm accused. Bail may also be granted at any stage of investigation, inquiry or trial if the officer or court finds that there are no reasonable grounds to believe the accused has committed a non‑bailable offence but there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry; in such cases the accused may be released on bail or on a bond without sureties. Finally, after the trial has concluded but before judgment is delivered, if the court believes there are reasonable grounds to think the accused is not guilty, it must release the accused on a bond without sureties.

citations.quote: When any person accused of any non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police-station, or appears or is brought before a Court, he may be released on bail, but he shall not be so released if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that he has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or transportation for life: Provided that the Court may direct that any person under the age of sixteen years or any woman or any sick or infirm person accused of such an offence be released on bail.

If it appears to such officer or Court at any stage of the investigation, inquiry or trial, as the case may be, that there are not reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed a non-bailable offence, but that there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry into his guilt, the accused shall, pending such inquiry, be released on bail, or, at the discretion of such officer or Court, on the execution by him of a bond without sureties for his appearance as hereinafter provided.

If, at any time after the conclusion of the trial of a person accused of a non-bailable offence and before judgment is delivered, the Court is of opinion that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of any such offence, it shall release the accused, if he is in custody on the execution by him of a bond without sureties for his appearance to hear judgment delivered.

text: Yes. The amount of a bail bond can be reduced, and this can be ordered by the High Court Division or a Court of Session.

citations.quote: the High Court Division or Court of Session may, in any case, whether there be an appeal on conviction or not, direct that any person be admitted to bail, or that the bail required by a police-officer or Magistrate be reduced.

text: When an inquiry or trial is concluded, the court may order the property produced before it to be disposed of as it thinks fit—by destruction, confiscation, delivery to any person claiming entitlement, or any other manner it deems appropriate.

citations.quote: the Court may make such order as it thinks fit for the disposal by destruction, confiscation, or delivery to any person claiming to be entitled to possession thereof or otherwise of any property or document produced before it

text: The High Court Division retains its inherent power to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under the Code, to prevent abuse of the process of any Court, and otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

citations.quote: Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent power of the High Court Division to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code, or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

text: A District Magistrate, or any other Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the Government or the District Magistrate to act under section 144, may issue such an order in an urgent case.

citations.quote: In cases where, in the opinion of a District Magistrate, [or any other Executive Magistrate] specially empowered by the Government or the District Magistrate to act under this section, ... such Magistrate may ... direct any person to abstain from a certain act

text: When a dispute over land (or water, buildings, crops, etc.) is likely to cause a breach of the peace, a District Magistrate or an Executive Magistrate specially empowered by the Government may, after being satisfied from a police report or other information, issue a written order. The order must state the grounds for his satisfaction, require the parties to appear before his court (in person or by pleader) within a time he fixes, and compel them to give written statements of their respective claims regarding possession. The Magistrate then examines those statements, hears the parties, receives and considers any evidence, may take further evidence, and decides which party was in possession on the date of the order. If he finds that a party was forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed, he may treat that party as being in possession and issue an order declaring that party entitled to possession until lawfully evicted, prohibiting any disturbance of that possession.

citations.quote: he shall make an order in writing, stating the grounds of his being so satisfied, and requiring the parties concerned in such dispute to attend his Court in person or by pleader, within a time to be fixed by such Magistrate, and to put in written statements of their respective claims as respects the fact of actual possession of the subject of dispute.

The Magistrate shall then, without reference to the merits or the claims of any of such parties to a right to possess the subject of dispute, peruse the statements so put in, hear the parties, receive all such evidence as may be produced by them respectively, consider the effect of such evidence, take such further evidence (if any) as he thinks necessary, and, if possible, decide whether any and which of the parties was at the date of the order before mentioned in such possession of the said subject

If the Magistrate decides that one of the parties was or should under the first proviso to sub-section (4) be treated as being in such possession of the said subject, he shall issue an order declaring such party to be entitled to possession thereof until evicted therefrom in due course of law, and forbidding all disturbance of such possession until such eviction

text: A magistrate may require a person to execute a bond for keeping the peace when he is informed that the person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb public tranquillity, or to do any wrongful act that may probably occasion such a breach, and the magistrate, in his opinion, has sufficient ground for proceeding. He may also do so when he has reason to believe that the person is likely to commit such a breach and that the breach cannot be prevented except by detaining the person in custody, after recording his reasons.

citations.quote: Whenever [a District Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate] is informed that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity or to do any wrongful act that may probably occasion a breach of the peace, ... the Magistrate if in his opinion there is sufficient ground for proceeding may ... require such person to show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond, with or without sureties, for keeping the peace

(1) has reason to believe that any person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity ... and that such breach of the peace or disturbance cannot be prevented otherwise than by detaining such person in custody, such Magistrate may, after recording his reasons, issue a warrant for his arrest ... and may send him before a Magistrate empowered to deal with the case

text: Yes. When a police‑officer makes an arrest without a warrant, the law requires that the arrested person be taken, without unnecessary delay, before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police‑station.

citations.quote: A police-officer making an arrest without warrant shall, without unnecessary delay and subject to the provisions herein contained as to bail, take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police-station.

text: The officer must give the subordinate a written order that specifies the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for the arrest.

citations.quote: he shall deliver to the officer required to make the arrest an order in writing, specifying the person to be arrested and the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made.

text: Yes. When a person is arrested, the officer making the arrest (or the police‑officer to whom a private arrest is handed over) may search the arrested person and seize any articles found on him, except necessary clothing.

citations.quote: may search such person, and place in safe custody all articles, other than necessary wearing‑apparel, found upon him

text: A person arrested without a warrant may be detained for up to twenty‑four hours before a magistrate must authorize any further detention.

citations.quote: shall not, in the absence of a special order of a Magistrate under section 167, exceed twenty-four hours

text: For a cognizable offence, the police officer must put the information in writing, have it read back to the informant and entered in the police‑station book, and may then investigate the case without first obtaining a magistrate’s order. For a non‑cognizable offence, the officer also records the information in the police‑station book, but must refer the informant to a magistrate and may not investigate the case unless a magistrate of the first or second class orders him to do so.

citations.quote: Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence if given orally to an officer in charge of a police-station, shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the Government may prescribe in this behalf.

When information is given to an officer in charge of a police-station of the commission within the limits of such station of a non-cognizable offence, he shall enter in a book to be kept as aforesaid the substance of such information and refer the informant to the Magistrate.
No police-officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate of the first or second class having power to try such case or [send] the same for trial.

text: The police must tell the person being arrested the reasons for the arrest, and they must put those reasons in writing at the time of the arrest.

citations.quote: Every police-officer arresting any person without warrant shall, at the time of making arrest, communicate to him the reasons for which he is arrested.
the police-officer shall record while making such arrest, his reasons in writing

text: For offences that are not classified as non‑bailable (i.e., bailable offences), the law requires that a person who is prepared to give bail must be released on bail, although the officer or court may instead discharge him on a bond without sureties. For non‑bailable offences, bail is only discretionary: the person may be released on bail unless there are reasonable grounds to believe he has committed a capital offence (punishable with death or transportation for life), and the court may also release him on a bond without sureties if there are insufficient grounds to hold him for trial.

citations.quote: When any person other than a person accused of a non-bailable offence ... is ... prepared ... to give bail, such person shall be released on bail
Provided that such officer or Court, if he or it thinks fit, may, instead of taking bail ... discharge him on his executing a bond without sureties

After a person is arrested, the law requires that he be brought before the magistrate who has jurisdiction (section 86). The magistrate first checks that the arrested person is the one named in the warrant and then either directs his removal to the court that issued the warrant or, if the offence is bailable, takes bail or security and forwards the bond to that court. If the offence is non‑bailable, the magistrate may, after recording reasons, release the accused on interim bail and order him to appear before the issuing court. 

Once before the magistrate, the magistrate (or any magistrate specially empowered) may record any statement or confession made by the accused (section 164). The recorded statement or confession is signed and forwarded to the magistrate who will conduct the inquiry or trial. 

When the trial date is fixed, the court proceeds to take all evidence in support of the prosecution (section 265G). If during the proceeding a different magistrate takes over, he may use the evidence already recorded by his predecessor, or may re‑summon witnesses and re‑record evidence (section 350). 

If the accused appears before the magistrate and is found capable of making his defence, the inquiry or trial continues (section 468). After conviction, the court records the facts of the offence, any statement made by the offender, the finding and the sentence (section 481).

text: The Code of Criminal Procedure now permits a police‑officer to make an arrest without a warrant in several situations.  A police‑officer may arrest, without a magistrate’s order, (i) any person who commits a cognizable offence in the officer’s presence, and (ii) any person against whom a reasonable complaint, credible information or reasonable suspicion exists that he has committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of up to seven years, provided the officer believes the person has committed the offence and that the arrest is necessary for investigation, to prevent further offence, to preserve evidence or to prevent intimidation (section 54(1)).  The provision also lists additional categories of persons who may be arrested without warrant, such as those against whom credible information shows they have committed a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment of more than seven years or death, persons in possession of implements of house‑breaking, proclaimed offenders, persons found with suspected stolen property, those who obstruct police, deserters from the armed forces, persons involved in extraterritorial offences liable to extradition, and released convicts breaching certain rules (section 54(e)).  An arrest may also be made on a requisition from another police‑officer that specifies the person and the offence, if it appears that the person could lawfully be arrested without a warrant by the officer who issued the requisition (section 54(3)).  The Code expressly forbids using this power for preventive detention (section 54(2)).  When an arrest is made without a warrant, the officer must record the reasons in writing and must at the time of arrest communicate those reasons to the person arrested (section 54A).

A Magistrate shall, before recording any such confession, explain to the person making it that he is not bound to make a confession and that if he does so it may be used as evidence against him and no Magistrate shall record any such confession unless, upon questioning the person making it, he has reason to believe that it was made voluntarily; and, when he records any confession, he shall make a memorandum at the foot of such record to the following effect:- "I have explained to (name) that he is not bound to make a confession ..."
